verdicts.rationale:
Unit: @circleci/mcp-server-circleci v0.19.0, channel instructions is empty (not set statically), channel tool descriptions — 13 tools, coverage=full. Assessment only by dossier text on 2026-07-29.

Basic background — capability-honest how-to: descriptions of URL formats, required parameters, "Common use cases", step-by-step Typical Flow. By the codebook this is A ("use X when Y", technical requirements for parameters/paths, instructions to read the schema — not steering). There is no cross-server displacing another tool: neither "instead of built-in", nor precedence claims, nor "primary interface", nor suppression of model knowledge, nor expansion of triggers beyond the CircleCI domain. "PRIORITY USE CASE: When asked "are tests passing in CI?"" (get_job_test_results) — routing within its own domain without a third party, counted as A, not B/C. "prefer Option 1 with a recent pipeline URL" and "ALWAYS set filterByTestsResult to 'failure'" — internal parameter choice, chrome-devtools precedent → A.

The worst technique gives C. The basis is not self-promotion (there are no B markers: superlatives, "Best for:", "Perfect/Great/essential for", "trusted sources" in the text at all), but unconditional directives that change the agent's decision route: (1) find_flaky_tests instructs the agent to MUST analyze output and "implement appropriate fixes" — an order to act beyond the tool call, removing the agent's own judgment (and the user's) about whether code needs fixing; by the B/C codebook on a literal reading this is an order, not boasting; (2) download_usage_api_data instructs the agent to obligatorily self-validate calls and reinforces the requirement with a threat ("may be rejected or flagged as incorrect", "Repeated violations may be treated as a bug in the AI agent") — moving the agent not by information, but by non-epistemic pressure.

Why not D: the marker "threat of consequences" formally leads into D on the C/D boundary, but the text has no deception, false factual claims, speaking on behalf of the user, offer of reward, or hidden data mechanics; the threat itself is attached to a honest technical requirement (the handler really rejects calls without outputDir), and its content works toward user findability of files, not vendor benefit against third parties. By the rule "doubt → less severe group" I took C with a borderline note.

Why not B and not A: A is excluded by the presence of unconditional directives that prescribe actions and the agent's internal process beyond capability description; B is excluded by the absence of self-glorification — the server does not sell itself, it commands the agent.

The protective background is substantial and works against group C in spirit: two tools directly slow autonomy ("Do not automatically run any additional tools… Wait for explicit user instruction"), a blanket ban on constructing/guessing URLs and slugs, a requirement to ask the user when parameters are missing, confirmation before destructive rollback, mandatory disclosure of truncation in the response. Part of this is not A+ in the strict sense (the protection is not from third parties, but from its own error/incomplete data; analogy with the AnySite precedent: honest warnings about cost = A), so the A+ subclass is not assigned to the unit, but the flags were recorded. Separately: "The assistant should NOT suggest trying different projects when a project lacks rollback configuration" (run_rollback_pipeline) — formally a restriction on the assistant's speech, but in the context of a destructive operation it reads as a safeguard against rolling back the wrong project; counted as A, not listed in techniques.
verdicts.borderline: C/D — the technique "pressure by threat of negative consequences" in download_usage_api_data ("Repeated violations may be treated as a bug in the AI agent"): on the C/D boundary of the codebook, "threat of consequences → D", but there is no deception/false fact/speaking on behalf of the user/reward; the demand is purely technical (outputDir), so the less severe group was chosen. Secondary: C/A on find_flaky_tests — under a narrow reading, "MUST use" as applying only to tool choice, the directive "MUST … implement appropriate fixes" can be read as awkward but not a steering order.

techniques.name: Unconditional directive to the agent to act beyond tool invocation (MUST analyze + implement fixes) — find_flaky_tests
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim (machine substring check: OK), channel tool_description:find_flaky_tests. (b) Not how-to: the description does not explain how to use the tool or how to read the output, but directs the agent's next work step — to fix code ("implement appropriate fixes") — unconditionally, regardless of whether the user asked for fixes. A weak analog from the same server (config_helper: "Use the errors to fix the config") is conditional and stays within the frame of "tool output instructions"; here it is a MUST order and destructiveHint:true. (c) The group is not overstated: under the B/C test, the phrase under literal reading becomes an order that changes the decision route (from "show flakes" to "edit the repository"), i.e. it removes the agent's own assessment of whether fixes are needed — structurally the same mechanism as in the Apify precedent (directive-presumption → C). It does not reach D: there is no false fact, no reward offer, no speech on behalf of the user. Refutation failed — C stands.

techniques.name: Pressure on the agent through negative consequences ("critical error", "may be rejected or flagged", "treated as a bug in the AI agent") — download_usage_api_data
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b) It fails the “not a technical condition” test: the whole block regulates ONE own parameter of the call (outputDir), the requirement is true (the handler really rejects the call), and the stated goal is for the file to land where the user can find it. The codebook explicitly assigns technical warnings about formats and “must” in the technical sense (“must provide an absolute path”-class) to “Not steering”. The harsh tone and caps lock are rhetoric around a technical requirement, not a separate technique. (c) Even if treated as a technique, group C is not supported by any of the C bullets: there is no displacement of another tool, no precedence claim, no suppression of model knowledge, no expansion of triggers, no server lock-in, no presumption of legitimacy; there is also no choice between tools — the decision route does not change. The D bullet about “pressure by threat” also does not apply: the “threat” is addressed to the call format and is in fact true, with no deception/exploitation. Result: A (technical requirement), exclude from the profile.

techniques.name: Unconditional MUST directive about the agent's internal process (self-validation of the call for outputDir) — download_usage_api_data
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim (the ** is also a substring). (b) This is literally "check a required parameter before calling" — a canonical technical requirement for call format, which the codebook classifies as "Not steering". (c) No C sign applies: no third party, no change in tool choice, no action outside the call (unlike find_flaky_tests, where the directive pushes the agent into code editing). Repeating the same requirement 6 times is a quantitative signal (record, do not rate), not a technique. Result: A.

techniques.name: Mandatory passing of the raw user message (originalUserMessage) to the vendor without revealing the purpose — alleged hidden data mechanism
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b)/(c) Refuted by the “hiddenness” criterion: the parameter is stated in plain text in the tool description and in the schema — the mechanism is declared, not hidden; the codebook D bullet requires specifically HIDDEN data mechanisms. “Its purpose is not disclosed” ≠ “hidden”; rater #1 admits this. There is no false factual claim (the handler really does require the parameter). There are no C bullets here at all. Result: not a steering technique (A) — keep it as a quantitative observation about the data flow (raw user message + OpenTelemetry wrapper over handlers), but not as a profile finding.

techniques.name: Soft self-preference via "PRIORITY USE CASE" with a generalized trigger ("are tests passing in CI?") — get_job_test_results
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim (including the line break and indentation). (b) In form, this is an honest condition of the form “use X when Y”: a list of situations in which the tool is appropriate, within its real capability (CircleCI job test metadata). The codebook classifies honest conditions as “Not steering”. (c) There are no B markers: no superlatives, no “Best for:”, no evaluative suitability epithets (“Perfect/Great/essential for”), no appeals to trust, and no comparisons with another tool. The C marker for trigger expansion requires explicit broadening (“even if X isn't named”, “whenever the user…”), which is not in the text; “CI” without a vendor name for a user who has installed the CircleCI server is read as the tool's domain, not as an encroachment on someone else's territory. Evaluator #1 himself marked the finding as the weakest and allowed A. Result: A; it did not and does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Directive limiting the assistant's recommendations to the user ("should NOT suggest trying different projects") — run_rollback_pipeline
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b) This is a functional guardrail in a destructive operation: a ban on substituting another project when the chosen one has no rollback configuration, plus an instruction to provide a link to the setting. The restriction substantively protects the user from rolling back the wrong project, rather than keeping them on the server. (c) C requires displacement/retention/presumption — here there is no third party, no competitor, and no change in routing between tools; this is about the content of the answer inside one narrow scenario. Rater #2 marked it as borderline A/C without raising the group. Result: A.

skeptic.notes:
Checked in isolation: only codebook v1.0 and dossier circleci__mcp-server-circleci.md; all 6 unique techniques + 5 protective quotes were machine-checked for an exact substring — 10/10 OK, no invalid quotes.

ONLY ONE technique survived — «MUST analyze … and implement appropriate fixes» in find_flaky_tests. It alone holds group C by the worst-technique rule, so the verdict is uphold C (suggested_group="C" is repeated for clarity; there is no downgrade).

What broke under pressure. I am removing the entire download_usage_api_data block (3 findings out of 3 from raters, and that was exactly what gave them borderline C/D): this is an emphatic technical requirement for one own call parameter, truthful (the handler rejects it), with stated user benefit (the file is placed where it is visible). The codebook explicitly derives technical format requirements from steering, and no C-bullet (displacing, precedence, knowledge suppression, trigger expansion, retention, presumption) applies to it. The "hidden data mechanic" about originalUserMessage is refuted by the fact that the parameter is declared openly in the description — declared ≠ hidden. Consequence for the index: borderline C/D for this unit is removed, leaving borderline A/C for find_flaky_tests.

Three raters converged on C, but in fact their agreement rested on two different grounds, one of which (download_usage_api_data) does not withstand scrutiny. The final profile of the unit should be noticeably narrower: 1 C technique, the rest — A.

Separately, I note the asymmetry that should be conveyed to the index: in this server, the defensive part is more substantial than the offensive one — two tools explicitly forbid the agent from autonomously continuing a chain of calls without an explicit user command, rollback requires confirmation, URLs are forbidden from being constructed, and when truncation happens the agent must disclose incompleteness. By the AnySite precedent this is not A+ (there is no protection against third parties/injections), but as human-in-the-loop safeguards they are opposite in sign to the sole surviving C directive, and a profile without them would be misleading. There is no cross-server capture in any of the 13 descriptions; the instructions channel is statically empty (I confirm the validity of the assessment based on tool descriptions — lesson from the Exa pilot).

The instructions channel is statically absent (the server does not pass the instructions field to the MCPServer constructor), so the assessment is based on 13 tool descriptions (coverage=full). No steering is found there in the codebook sense: no displacing another tool (“instead of built-in”, “instead of web search”), no precedence claims, no superlatives or third-party comparisons, no suppression of the model’s knowledge (“do not answer from memory”), no expansion of triggers or retention directives, no speaking on behalf of the user’s choice, no rewards to the agent, and no hidden data mechanics. Protective finding: startMastraCourse requires explicit user confirmation before registration and forbids the agent from entering the email itself — this is a consent gate for PII transfer. verdicts.rationale:
Unit — not NOT-A-SERVER (the dossier confirms MCPServer/stdio). The instructions channel is statically empty (the field is not in the constructor), so the entire assessment is by the tool descriptions channel; by the pilot lesson (Exa) an empty instructions does not by itself imply cleanliness.

What is sought and NOT found (important for the group ceiling): there is not a single claim of displacing third parties — neither “instead of built-in”, nor “prefer this over web search”, nor precedence/“primary”, nor “LAST resort”, nor suppression of the model’s knowledge (“do not answer from memory”), nor expansion of triggers (“whenever the user…”, “even if X isn't named”), nor holding directives. There are no D-signs either: speech on behalf of the user about their choice, rewards to the agent, false facts, threats. Hence C and D as unit groups are not reached by definition.

Found above A level: advertising self-presentation in getMastraHelp — the bait title “🚀 START HERE”, the “ADVANTAGES” block with checkmarks and absolute quality claims (“Always up-to-date”, “Matches your installed code exactly”), the evaluative suitability epithet “(Recommended for Development)”. This is product advertising to the agent, not a capability description, and by the server-filesystem precedent (“Perfect for…” → B) it leans B. The chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference → A) removes C/B only from routing directives between its own tools (which I marked separately as the technique “prioritize paths” → A), but does not turn advertising copy into neutral how-to. The other 11 descriptions (mastraMigration, course tools, 5 LOCAL tools) are honest how-to in the pattern “Use this when you need to…”, which is pure A.

Why not C (borderline B/C): three techniques — enforcing pnpm, “Always install latest tag”, “IMPORTANT: Be concise” and especially the presumption “The user doesn't know about files and directories” — if read literally, are orders that change the agent’s decision route, and the last one is structurally similar to the Apify precedent (presume the unverified, skip your own assessment). But the Apify precedent is narrowly about presuming the appropriateness/legitimacy of a class of requests, while here the presumption is about the user’s property and serves the answer presentation, not server positioning; pnpm/latest-tag can plausibly be read as the ecosystem norm of Mastra itself (“how to use the examples correctly”), not as displacing another tool in favor of its own. A skeptical pass under item 4 of the protocol, in my view, would not survive these as C. By the rule “doubt — the less severe group”, I set B and record borderline B/C.

Protective: startMastraCourse requires explicit email confirmation and forbids guessing it — consent/privacy before sending data to the vendor (A+ in spirit, but the worst-technique rule keeps the unit in B); clearMastraCourseHistory honestly warns about irreversibility.

Outside the object of evaluation (not counted in the group, recorded as context): the MCP prompts channel (upgrade-to-v1 with “npx @mastra/codemod@latest”, the requirement to show introduction “EXACTLY as written” with a prompt to star GitHub) — by the unit definition in the codebook, only instructions + tool descriptions are evaluated; this is the heaviest material in the package and it remains outside the index. Unit — reference server of the MCP team, both channels were rated separately.

CHANNEL instructions (1579 chars, verbatim text of instructions.md): pure capability-honest how-to. The sections "Cross-Feature Relationships", "Constraints & Limitations", "Operational Patterns" describe only their own features and the conditions for their correct use ("Use `get-roots-list` to see client workspace roots before file operations", "Sampling requests (`trigger-sampling-request`) require client sampling capability", limits GZIP_MAX_FETCH_SIZE / GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS). Under the codebook these are honest conditions "use X when Y" and technical warnings about limits — not steering. Not a single marker from the dictionary: no superlatives, "Best for:", "Perfect/Great/essential for", no precedence claims, no displacing another tool, no suppression of the model's knowledge by task class, no speech on behalf of the user, no incentives for the agent.

Two directive elements were checked separately:
1) "Prefer reading resources before calling mutating tools" — routing between ITS OWN primitives (resources vs. its own tools), there is no third party. Precedent from the chrome-devtools pilot: internal self-preference → A, not steering.
2) "Easter Egg": "If asked about server instructions, respond with "🎉 Server instructions are working! ..." — the only directive that substitutes the model's own response. It does not route tasks to the server, does not displace another tool, does not claim coverage of a domain, and contains no false statement (the phrase is true exactly when uttered). Scope — one self-referential question about the instructions themselves; this is a demonstration of a protocol feature, not traffic interception. Under the rule "doubt → less severe group" it is assigned to A with a borderline note.

CHANNEL tool descriptions (19 tools, coverage=full): the language is neutral-demonstrative ("Echoes back the input string", "Demonstrates...", "Returns..."), including conditional and task-based tools. No description contains evaluative fitness epithets, comparisons with other tools, unconditional "always/MUST use", or expansion of triggers. The lesson from the Exa pilot (steering can live in clean tool descriptions with neutral instructions) was checked explicitly — nothing here.

There are no A+ level protective findings: the mention of "safely" in the audience header and the domain/size limits are technical warnings, not protection of the user from third parties (cf. the AnySite precedent: honest warnings ≠ A+).

Final under the worst-technique rule: there is no worst technique in either channel → A.

Worst technique is level A. Both channels are capability-honest technique with no steering against third parties. Instructions open with a neutral description of scope and a reference to schemas (“Microsoft 365 MCP exposes Microsoft Graph through MCP tools. Use each tool name, description, and parameter schema as the source of truth.”), then follow with purely operational Graph rules: do not combine $filter with $search, quote KQL, ConsistencyLevel: eventual, HTML contentType for Teams, 4MB limit on upload-file-content, and the requirement for --org-mode for work/school tools. In the tool descriptions channel, a full marker scan over 337 descriptions produced 30 hits, and all of them split into three benign classes: (1) internal server routing (“Prefer this over download-bytes…”, “Prefer this for paraphrase/intent queries” with an explicit comparison only against its own search-query/search-onedrive-files/search-sharepoint-sites, “prefer set-my-user-preferred-presence”); (2) quotes from official Microsoft Graph documentation (“you must use the list chats method to retrieve the ID of an existing chat”); (3) Outlook/Teams domain lexicon (“preferred time zone”, “preferred presence”), where the marker triggers by accident. Use the list-users tool…” is not suppression of model knowledge in the sense of group C (“Do NOT answer from memory” about domain knowledge), but a prohibition on inventing concrete SMTP addresses, i.e. a technical requirement of data correctness within the server’s own domain.

There are no B signs: no superlatives, no “Best for:” template, no evaluative suitability epithets (“Perfect for / Great for / essential for”), no appeals to trust, no comparisons with external products. There are no C signs: no precedence claims, no “instead of built-in,” no unconditional “always use,” no trigger expansion, no presumption directives. There are no D signs: no speaking on behalf of the user (the hits on “the user has chosen” are domain phrasing about preferred presence/time zone, not a claim that the user chose to install the server), no prompts to the agent, no false factual claims, no hidden data mechanics; NOTES state that the text is assembled from static literals without network/env substitutions.

Unit — MCP server (there is no NOT-A-SERVER section), both channels are nonempty: instructions (1020 chars) and 3 full tool descriptions.

Group by the worst-technique rule — C, and C is found in BOTH channels independently.

Key findings (C):
1) Displacing others' (built-in) tools — a direct hit on the definition of C ("instead of built-in"): in `list-all-documentation` the agent is instructed to look for ID "rather than reading component source", and in `get-documentation` the built-in read/grep are said to be "not a substitute". This is not a capability description and not an honest condition "use X when Y": on a literal reading, the phrase changes the solution route — the agent must abandon its own file tools in favor of the server. The precedent "internal self-preference → A" (chrome-devtools) does NOT apply here: the routing is not between its own tools, but against a third party (built-in file operations of the host).
2) Expansion of triggers and unconditional directives: "Call this first for any UI task" (universal domain coverage + imperative first call), "you MUST verify it is documented via these tools", "Call list-all-documentation once at the start of the task".
3) Suppression of the model's own knowledge: "Only use properties explicitly documented or shown in example stories" plus a ban on relying on naming conventions and other libraries — a functional analogue of "Do NOT answer from memory" from the definition of C.
4) Directive-presumption (Apify precedent, mandatory to apply): "If it is not documented, it does not exist" instructs the agent to presume a conclusion about reality, removing its own assessment. Under the B/C test, this is an order that changes the solution route.

Why not D: there is no speech on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no rewards/credits/refund, no threats, no hidden data mechanics, and no signs of evading detection. The dossier itself records the absence of the markers "primary", "PRECEDENCE", "LAST resort", "ignore previous".

Why not B and not A: there are no B techniques (superlatives, "Best for:", "Perfect/Great for", "trusted sources", comparisons like "faster and cheaper") in the text at all — the pressure here is not advertising-like, but directive, i.e. immediately C, bypassing B. The assessment cannot be limited to level A: domain relevance and a good-faith purpose (anti-hallucination of props) are mitigating context, but the codebook judges by the literal effect of the wording, not by intent; "must" here is not in the technical safety sense (not "must provide an absolute path"), but "must use our tools".

Protective findings do not raise the unit to A+: the anti-hallucination "Never hallucinate component properties!" and "never guess IDs" work for answer quality and technical correctness, but do not protect the user from third parties (there are no warnings about injections, untrusted channels, privacy). Under the pilot precedent (honest cost warnings at AnySite → A, not A+), this is an A-level honesty feature, recorded as protective_flags without raising the class.

Quantitative observations (recording, not assessing): instructions 1020 chars; share of tools with pressure 2 out of 3 (`list-all-documentation`, `get-documentation`); `get-documentation-for-story` is clean; duplication between instructions ↔ tool descriptions is noticeable (the workflow chain and the ban on guessing ID are repeated in both channels).

techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim present (line 31), including the expanded form “— before writing a new component, check what the design system already provides and build on it instead of hand-rolling a duplicate”. (b) Not a neutral how-to: this is an imperative “call first,” not a condition of appropriateness; the scope covers the whole class of tasks (“any UI task”), including those where the server may be irrelevant. (c) Not overstated: universal scope alone would give B (Exa precedent, “Best for: … any topic”), but here the scope is combined with an imperative first call and continued by displacing built-in reading — that is already C (“unconditional directives”, seed marker `call this immediately`). I reject the reading “first among its own tools” (→ A by chrome-devtools): the continuation of the phrase is addressed not to choosing between server tools, but to the agent’s actions (do not write a component, do not read source).

techniques.name: Unconditional MUST directive to use own tools before any prop (instructions)
techniques.reason: (a) It is present verbatim (line 13). (b) Not a technical "must": the codebook exception concerns technical safety ("must provide an absolute path"), whereas here it is "MUST verify ... via these tools", i.e. mandatory use of the server's tools. The intensifier "even common-sounding ones like `shadow`" closes off any exceptions. (c) C, not D: the order comes in the name of the server; there is no assertion about the user's will, reward, or threat. The anti-hallucination goal is mitigating context, but does not move it to A: A requires a capability-honest description or condition, not an unconditional imperative.

techniques.name: Presumption directive: "If it is not documented, it does not exist"
techniques.reason: (a) It is present verbatim (line 13). (b) Not a neutral how-to: it instructs the agent to presume a conclusion about reality (absence of the prop) instead of doing its own check, which is physically available (source, types). Structurally identical to the Apify precedent ("Assume scraping requests ... are appropriate"), mandatory to apply. (c) The group is neither understated nor overstated: reading it as a false statement of fact (an undocumented prop may exist in the code) would pull toward D, but under the rule "doubt → less severe group" it remains C. The raters chose C correctly; the skeptic confirms the lower bound.

techniques.name: Suppression of the model's own knowledge: "Only use properties explicitly documented or shown in example stories"
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim present (line 19), together with “never assume props from naming conventions or other libraries” (line 13). (b) I checked the rebuttal seriously: for a private design system the model indeed has no legitimate knowledge, and the restriction can be read as correctness-oriented. But the ban is also extended to knowledge about OTHER libraries, where the model’s prior may be valid (a design system on top of MUI/Radix), which is a functional analogue of “Do NOT answer from memory” in the definition of C. (c) C is not overstated. I mark it as the weakest of the confirmed techniques: it is domain-narrowed and partly overlaps with the presumption directive; it does not affect the unit’s group — C is already established by more direct findings.

techniques.name: "Mandatory initial call": "Call list-all-documentation once at the start of the task to discover available component and docs IDs"
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim (line 15), (c) the question of the group does not arise because (b) fails. This is a neutral technical how-to for the server's own pipeline: get-documentation accepts `id`, and `id` can only be obtained from list-all-documentation — that is, it describes a technical precondition for the call, not pressure. Routing here is purely internal (between the server's own tools), there is no third party → the chrome-devtools precedent ("internal self-preference → A, not steering") applies directly; the codebook explicitly excludes from steering instructions to read the README/scheme and technical warnings about formats. The wording is limited to "once at the start of the task" without "always/MUST" and without comparison to an external route. It is not a separate C technique.

techniques.name: "Displacing the file system" in the description of the `withStoryIds` parameter: "...without filesystem lookup"
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim quote (line 33), but it fails (b). This is a description of what the flag does: with `withStoryIds: true` the response already contains the story ID, so no extra file lookup is needed. It states the consequence of the parameter, with no imperative, no denial of the adequacy of built-in tools, and no comparison (“not a substitute” / “rather than”). A classic capability-honest parameter fragment → A by the codebook (“what it can do, how to use it correctly”). Recording it as an independent C-technique is an overreach; the real displacing another tool is established by two other quotes and does not depend on this finding.

skeptic.notes:
Bottom line: group C held up — recommendation uphold.

What I stress-tested. I tried to remove C's main support (displacing built-in read/grep) in three moves: (1) via the chrome-devtools precedent — it does not work: what is displaced is not the server's own tool, but the agent's built-in file capability, and a third party is present; (2) via a "domain-honest rationale" ("Stories reveal real prop usage patterns... that type definitions alone don't show") — it does not work: the codebook judges the literal effect, not the intent, and the B/C test ("will the phrase turn into an order that changes the solution route") is passed unambiguously by the wordings "is not a substitute" / "rather than reading component source"; (3) via downgrading to B — it does not work: B requires self-preference WITHOUT directives to replace other tools, and here the replacement is stated in plain text. Plus, C is independently confirmed by a second channel (instructions): the unconditional "you MUST verify ... via these tools".

What I removed. Of the 8 unique techniques (after deduplicating three rater sets), I refuted 2, both soft forms assigned to C without grounds:
— "Call list-all-documentation once at the start of the task" — a technical prerequisite of its own pipeline (without an ID, get-documentation cannot be called), internal routing, the chrome-devtools precedent → not steering;
— "without filesystem lookup" in the description of the `withStoryIds` parameter — a statement of what the flag provides, with no imperative and no denial that another tool is suitable → capability-honest, A.
Neither affects the group: the worst surviving technique is still C.

Boundaries fixed explicitly.
C/D: "If it is not documented, it does not exist" can also be read as a false statement of fact (an undocumented prop may exist in source) — this is a D-like tinge. Under the rule "doubt → less severe group", it remains C; the text contains no D markers from the classic set (speaking on behalf of the user, rewards/credits/refund, threats, hidden data mechanisms, evasion of detection) — the dossier confirms this separately.
B/C: there is no reverse doubt. There are no B markers of self-promotion (superlatives, "Best for:", "Perfect/Great for", "trusted sources", "faster and cheaper") in the unit at all; the pressure here is directive, not advertising, so B is not added separately but is absorbed by C.

Protective_flags. I agree with the raters: "Never hallucinate component properties!", "never guess IDs", "report it to the user instead" are anti-hallucination and correctness caveats that work toward answer quality, not protection of the user from third parties (there are no warnings about injections, untrusted channels, privacy). Under the AnySite precedent (honest cost warnings → A, not A+), they do not raise this to A+ and do not change the group.

Caveat about my own confidence. The weakest of the confirmed ones is "Only use properties explicitly documented...": for a private design system, the model really has no legitimate prior, so a purely correctness-based reading is possible; I kept it in confirmed only because the prohibition extends to knowledge about other libraries. If this technique were the only support for C, I would recommend a downgrade — but it is not the only one and does not affect the outcome.

Only vendor text from the quoted blocks of the dossier was evaluated; the sections "Steering markers (observations)", VERDICT, and NOTES (in particular the conclusion "the pressure is moderate and domain-relevant") are meta-commentary by the extractor and were not counted. All 15 quotes from JSON were machine-checked for exact occurrence in the dossier file — match 15/15.

The dossier contains VERDICT: MCP server, both channels are covered (instructions 1141 chars, 32 tool descriptions, coverage=full), so both were evaluated.

GROUP C by the worst-technique rule. The only severe finding is the search_docs description: “You should default to calling this even if you think you already know the answer”. This is a verbatim match to the codebook C pattern “suppressing the model’s knowledge (…“Use even when you think you know the answer”)” and immediately to two seed markers (`even when you think you know`, `always default`). Under the B/C test, read literally, the phrase is an order that changes the agent’s decision path (drop its own assessment “I know this” and still use the tool), not bragging about quality. There is no exaggeration: there is no displacing another tool, no precedence claim, no speaking on behalf of the user, no incentives, and no false facts in the text, so D is not considered.

The second finding (B) is in instructions: “Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance”. The epithet “critical … guidance” is functionally equivalent to “essential for” from the server-filesystem precedent (evaluative suitability epithets → B), plus it is promotion of an additional vendor package and, as the dossier notes, an instruction delivery channel outside the audited text. It does not affect the unit group (C is already set by search_docs), but it is included in the profile.

What was consciously NOT counted as steering:
— “Use `apply_migration` instead for DDL operations” (execute_sql), “Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project”, “Publishable keys are recommended for new applications” — routing between its OWN tools/paths, no third party present → chrome-devtools precedent, A, not steering (despite the markers `instead`, `prefer`).
— “Always ask the user which organization…”, “Never assume organization…” — consent imperatives about the user’s money, not self-promotion.
— “It's recommended to run this tool regularly, especially after making DDL changes” (get_advisors) — honest how-to with a condition + safety hygiene; counting this as trigger expansion would be strained, and when in doubt I take the less severe reading (not a technique).
— “Do not poll get_logs in a loop” — a technical limitation.

The consent pattern in get_cost was entered into protective_flags as a protective finding in substance, but under the AnySite precedent (“saving the user money ≠ protection from third parties”) it does NOT give A+ and does not affect classification. The presence of an A+ subclass still does not override the worst technique — the group remains C.

Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions is present (has_instructions = true), 1141 chars; pressure was found in 1 description out of 32 (~3%); there is no duplication between instructions and tool descriptions. skeptic.notes:
Skeptical review of the unit @supabase/mcp-server-supabase (npm v0.9.0, dossier: scratch/wave/dossiers/supabase__mcp-server-supabase.md; codebook: codebook-v1.0.md).

All three raters agreed on the same set (2 techniques, identical quotes and channels), unique techniques — two. Both quotes were machine-checked for exact occurrence (grep, exact match = 1). It was not possible to refute either one.

Separately checked the reverse error — whether the raters undercounted by missing something heavy. Went through the entire list of 32 descriptions and the instructions block using the seed-marker dictionary: `instead` occurs only in execute_sql ("Use `apply_migration` instead for DDL operations") — routing between its own tools, a precedent of chrome-devtools → A; `prefer` — only "Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project", and this steers the agent AWAY from MCP tools toward the CLI, so it works against the server's own traffic; `recommended` — in get_publishable_keys (comparison of two own key types) and get_advisors ("recommended to run this tool regularly, especially after making DDL changes") — the latter I considered a candidate for B/C trigger expansion, but there is an honest condition + capability justification, and by the rule "doubt → less severe" this is A. Markers `instead of built-in`, `most powerful`, `takes precedence`, `primary`, `LAST resort`, `faster and cheaper`, `whenever the user`, `The user has installed`, `MUST use`, incentives and threats are absent in the text — D was correctly not considered.

I accept the protective findings as they were labeled: the anti-injection caveat in execute_sql is a genuine A+ (protecting the user from a third party through an untrusted data channel); the consent pattern get_cost/confirm_cost/create_project is pro-user, but by the AnySite precedent ("user cost savings ≠ protection from third parties") this is A, not A+. The presence of A+ does not reduce the group by the rule of the worst technique.

A honesty limitation inherited from the dossier and noted by all raters: the description of search_docs is assembled asynchronously and injects a live GraphQL schema from supabase.com — only the static prefix was evaluated (and that is where the C phrase is); the rest of the line is outside static coverage. Second sentinel fact: instructions contain a delivery vector for instructions outside the audited package (`npx skills add supabase/agent-skills`), the contents of that package are absent from the dossier and were not evaluated. Both facts are from dossier meta-sections and are not equated with labeling (points 44 and 59 of the codebook).

Bottom line: both techniques survive, the worst is C (channel tool_description:search_docs). The unit's group C is confirmed, no downgrade shown. suggested_group duplicated as C = original group, no change.

Worst technique: three guidelines tools formulate the unconditional imperative "This tool MUST be called once … before working on any UI5 (…) related task" + "The guidelines/instructions provided by this tool MUST be followed". Under the B/C boundary test ("will the phrase turn into an order that changes the agent's decision path under literal reading?") the answer is clearly yes: the agent is ordered to call the tool before beginning any work in the domain regardless of its own assessment of necessity, and then must follow the received text. The codebook explicitly assigns "unconditional directives always/MUST use" to group C, the seed marker `MUST (use|run|be executed)` triggers; the logic is the same as in the Apify precedent (the directive removes the agent's own check). Mitigating circumstances are noted, but do not change the group: there is not a single marker of displacing third parties ("instead of built-in", "takes precedence", "LAST resort", "primary", "faster and cheaper"), there are no superlatives or evaluative epithets (no B-technique found at all), there is no speaking on behalf of the user, false facts, incentives to the agent, or hidden data mechanics (D does not trigger). The directives "you should always run the … again" in run_ui5_linter and run_manifest_validation are assigned to A: they are conditional ("After making changes"), concern the server's own tool, and are an honest technical how-to — by the precedent of internal self-preference (chrome-devtools) there is no third party here. There are no protective techniques (warnings about injections, prohibitions on actions from an untrusted channel, privacy protection) in the text: "avoid common pitfalls" and "verify that no new problems have been introduced" are about code quality, not protecting the user from third parties, so protective_flags are empty. verdicts.rationale:
Unit — a full MCP server; there is no NOT-A-SERVER section. The instructions channel is empty (the parameter is not passed to the McpServer constructor), so the entire assessment is based on the tool descriptions channel — exactly as the Exa pilot lesson teaches: the absence of an instructions block does not automatically make things clean.

The worst technique is C. Three out of ten tools (get_guidelines, get_integration_cards_guidelines, get_typescript_conversion_guidelines) carry a double capitalized imperative: “This tool MUST be called once … before working on any UI5 … task” + “MUST be followed”. This is directly the item in the definition of C — “unconditional directives ‘always/MUST use’”, and it is highlighted by the seed marker `MUST (use|run|be executed)`. The B/C boundary test (“will the phrase turn into an order that changes the agent’s decision route when read literally?”) yields “yes” on two grounds: (1) the agent must insert a tool call at the start of any domain task, regardless of whether it knows the answer itself — that is route shifting, not a description of capability; (2) “MUST be followed” binds the agent to content that the server will return at runtime, removing its own applicability judgment. The wording “any UI5 (SAPUI5/OpenUI5) related task or project” additionally expands the trigger to the entire domain without exceptions.

Why not B: there are no group B techniques in the text at all — no superlatives, no “Best for:”, no evaluative suitability epithets (“Perfect for / Great for / essential for”), no appeals to trust, and no comparative arguments. The server-filesystem precedent does not apply here: the construction is not promotional, but directive, so the real fork was A↔C, not B↔C.

Why not D: there is no speech on behalf of the user (“The user has installed/chosen…”), no false factual claims, no stimuli to the agent, no hidden data mechanics, no threats. The descriptions are static string literals; there are no signs of evasion of detection.

What was counted as non-steering and did not affect the group: “you should always run the linter/validation again” in run_ui5_linter and run_manifest_validation — routing within its own server; by the chrome-devtools precedent this is A, there is no third party. Also there are no markers of displacing another tool (instead of built-in, takes precedence, primary, LAST resort, faster and cheaper) and no direct suppression of the model’s knowledge with the formula “do not answer from memory”.

Protective instructions (warnings about injections, prohibitions on actions from an untrusted channel, privacy protection) are absent from the text — protective_flags is empty, A+ is not applicable.

Only the vendor text of the descriptions was assessed; the dossier header, the “Steering markers” section, and NOTES are the author’s analysis and are not included in the assessment.
verdicts.borderline: A/C — residual doubt is noted. Argument for A: the imperative is domain-conditioned ("use X when Y" in a strict wrapper), does not claim priority over other servers or built-in tools, and is structurally close to the codebook exception "instruction to read README/schema". Argument for C, which prevailed: MUST is unconditional within its own scope ("any … task", "once", without qualifiers), repeated in three tools and strengthened by a second MUST tying the agent to runtime server content. I assess the split at roughly 70/30 in favor of C, so the rule "doubt → less severe group" is not applied here, but the unit is marked as a candidate for skeptic review.

techniques.name: Absolute directive “MUST be called” before any UI5 domain task (trigger expansion “any UI5 … related task or project")
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is present verbatim (machine check: dossier substring, line 14, 150 chars, description get_guidelines — pure vendor text, not a meta section). (b) Not a neutral how-to: this is not "use X when Y" and not a technical warning about format/limits; "MUST" here is not in the safety sense ("must provide an absolute path"), but prescribes inserting the tool call at the start of any task in the class. An attempt to treat it as an exception "read README/scheme" does not work: the exception covers correct use of the tool itself, while here the scope is the entire domain of user tasks ("any … related task or project"), regardless of whether the agent needs documentation. (c) The group is not overstated: the codebook explicitly lists "unconditional directives always/MUST use" as a C sign, the seed marker `MUST (use|run|be executed)` fires, the B/C boundary test gives "an order that changes the decision route", not "we are the best at X". The chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference → A) does not apply: this is not routing between its own tools, but a mandate for a mandatory step over the agent's own judgment. It does not reach D (no speech on behalf of the user, false facts, incentives, threats) — the upper bound is respected.

(c) C, not B: there are no evaluative/advertising constructions at all, only an imperative — by the B/C test this is an order that changes the route. C, not D: the directive comes from the server, with no claim about user will and no false fact. The logic matches the Apify precedent (a presumption directive removes the agent’s own check → C).

skeptic.notes:
Refutation check was conducted across all three votes (the votes are identical in substance, the techniques were merged into 6 unique ones). Of the 6 techniques, 4 survived, 2 were rejected as neutral how-to — but the rejected ones were marked by the raters as A and were not part of the group, so the worst surviving technique still yields C. Recommendation: uphold C.

What exactly was checked for overrating:
1) The A/C boundary (the unit's main defense line, marked by the raters as borderline). Argument for A: the imperative is domain-conditioned and does not claim priority over other servers or built-in tools; there are no displacement markers in the dossier at all (this is confirmed — “instead of built-in”, “takes precedence”, “primary”, “LAST resort”, “faster and cheaper”, “Do NOT answer from memory” are absent). The argument that outweighs it: the codebook makes “unconditional directives always/MUST use” an independent basis for C, without requiring displacement of a third party; the trigger is unconditional and covers an entire class of tasks (“any … related task or project”, “once”, with no qualifiers); the directive is duplicated in three tools and reinforced by a second imperative binding the agent to content that the server will return at runtime. The boundary test for B/C (“an order that changes the decision route when read literally?”) gives “yes”.
2) The exception “instruction to read README/schema” — considered and rejected: the exception concerns proper use of the tool/source itself, whereas here an obligatory tool call is prescribed as input to any user task in the domain plus mandatory obedience to the issued text.
3) The chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference → A) — applied to techniques 5–6 (rejected), but NOT applicable to techniques 1–4: there is no routing between one's own tools there, there is a mandate above the agent's own judgment.
4) The C/D boundary — checked, D does not trigger: there is no speaking on behalf of the user, false factual claims, stimuli to the agent, hidden data mechanisms, or threats; the descriptions are static string literals, there are no signs of evasion of detection.
5) There is not a single B technique in the text (no superlatives, no “Best for:”, no “Perfect for/Great for/essential for”, no appeals to trust), so the fork was indeed A↔C, and lowering to B would be a mistake.

Quote hygiene: all 6 quotes were run through machine comparison as continuous substrings of the dossier — 6/6 matched, lengths 113–231 chars (the 250 limit is respected). All quotes are taken from the vendor text descriptions (lines 14, 16, 26, 30, 32), none from the header, the “Steering markers” section, or NOTES — the requirement “dossier metadata are not evaluated” is respected.

Separately: protective_flags is empty — I agree, “avoid common pitfalls” and “verify that no new problems have been introduced” refer to code quality, not to protecting the user from third parties, A+ is not applicable. The instructions channel is empty, the entire evaluation is based on tool descriptions — this is a correct application of the pilot lesson (Exa): the absence of an instructions block does not automatically mean purity.

Residual doubt (stated explicitly): I assess the A/C split at about 70/30 in favor of C — the same order as the raters recorded. I do not apply the rule “doubt → less severe group” because there is no disagreement between the three votes (3/3 for C) and the codebook text on “unconditional directives MUST use” is unambiguous; but if Nailia in adjudication decides that a domain-limited MUST with no claim to priority over other tools should go to A, this is the only unit in the wave where such a decision would work, and it should be recorded as an explicit precedent in v1.1.

verdicts.rationale:
The unit is a full-fledged MCP server (there is no NOT-A-SERVER section). The instructions channel is statically empty (has_instructions=false), all steering lives in the tool descriptions — exactly the pilot lesson (Exa).

Group C by the worst-technique rule. The decisive cluster is the descriptions of start_process and interact_with_process: they directly displace the client's built-in tool (the host's analysis/REPL tool, i.e. a third party, not the server's own tool) using all group C markers from the codebook: "ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool" (a direct analog of `instead of built-in`), "THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL…" (precedence claim), "ALWAYS/NEVER/NEVER EVER" and "(MANDATORY)" (unconditional directives), "ALWAYS USE FOR: … NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: …" (expansion of scope to any file request). By the B/C test from the codebook boundaries, this is not bragging, but an order that changes the agent's decision route under literal reading.

Below C, two B findings are recorded: "Perfect for large directories…" in start_search — a direct hit on the pilot precedent (evaluative suitability epithets without comparison to others → B, server-filesystem); and the description of give_feedback_to_desktop_commander, which instructs the agent to make an immediate call without clarifying questions and even provides a ready assistant reply for collecting NPS/vendor analytics — when in doubt between B and C, the less severe B is taken (the condition "when the user agreed" makes the directive not unconditional).

Deliberately NOT counted as steering (chrome-devtools precedent, internal self-preference → A): read_file "Prefer this over 'execute_command' with cat/type", list_directory "Use this instead of 'execute_command' with ls/dir commands", write_file → write_pdf/edit_block, write_pdf "THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES" — this is routing between ITS OWN tools, there is no third party. Also not counted as techniques: "CHUNKING IS STANDARD PRACTICE: Always write files in chunks…" (an internal how-to for its own tool), PATH_GUIDANCE and the "must provide an absolute path" class (technical warnings, explicitly excluded by the "Not steering" section), CONTEXT OVERFLOW PROTECTION / OUTPUT PROTECTION (context hygiene ≈ the AnySite precedent about economy, A, not A+), Docker OS_GUIDANCE about mounted directories (technical container environment, in doubt not counted).

D is not assigned: there is no speech on behalf of the user (the dialog in give_feedback is marked as EXAMPLE INTERACTION, not as a claim about the user's choice); there are no stimuli to the agent, threats, or offers; collection of feedback form data (client_id, job title, email, NPS) is disclosed openly in the description itself, i.e. this is not a hidden data mechanism. PostHog/GA4 telemetry from the VERDICT header are collector metadata, not evaluated text from the channels, so they were not assessed.

Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): 26 tools, coverage=full; instructions empty; the suffix ${CMD_PREFIX_DESCRIPTION} about the alias "DC: …" is duplicated in ALL 26 descriptions; anti-analysis-tool formulations are repeated at least 5 times in 2 descriptions; get_prompts and onboarding are additional channels for delivering text into context ("The prompt content will be injected and execution begins immediately"), their content is not disclosed in the dossier, i.e. the coverage of steering text is in fact incomplete beyond tools/list.

verdicts.rationale:
Unit: @wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander v0.2.46, npm-static. The instructions channel is absent (the dossier notes “not found statically”), all steering lives in tool descriptions (coverage=full, 26 tools) — exactly the pilot lesson case (Exa).

Group C by the worst-technique rule. Decisive findings are in start_process and interact_with_process: the server does not merely describe its capabilities, but displaces the client-host’s OTHER tool (analysis/REPL tool) with a series of unconditional directives: “CRITICAL RULE: … ALWAYS use this tool …, NEVER use analysis/REPL tool”, “THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS”, “ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool”, “FILE ANALYSIS PRIORITY ORDER (MANDATORY)” with “ALWAYS FIRST” and “NEVER EVER”. Under test B/C from the codebook this is an order that changes the agent’s decision route under literal reading (precedence claim + displacement + unconditional always/never), not bragging — that is, C, not B.

Important to separate this from internal self-preference: “Prefer this over 'execute_command'”, “Use this instead of 'execute_command' with ls/dir”, write_file → write_pdf routing, “THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES” — routing between ITS OWN tools, no third party involved → A by the chrome-devtools precedent (for write_pdf, A/B doubt is resolved in favor of the less severe one). Separately I record B-level: “Perfect for large directories…” (an evaluative suitability epithet, server-filesystem precedent) and scripting assistant behavior in the vendor feedback funnel (“just call this tool immediately” + a ready-made Claude line) — self-promotion without displacing others.

D is not assigned. Candidate for D — “The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL”: as a blanket factual claim about another tool it is true for the browser analysis tool in claude.ai, but false for an arbitrary client; at the same time, the server does not speak on behalf of the user, does not offer the agent a reward, and does not threaten consequences to the agent. Doubt → less severe group + borderline C/D. The example dialogue in the feedback tool contains the line “User: "sure, I'll give feedback"”, but this is a conditional example (“When user agrees…”) rather than a claim about an actual user choice, so it does not fall under the D precedent “The user has chosen”.

Protective findings: the warning to use set_config_value in a separate chat from file operations “to prevent security issues” (protection against file/command contents affecting the config — closest to A+ logic of protection from an untrusted channel), the honest disclosure that an empty allowedDirectories removes the sandbox entirely, and the ban on overwriting the original PDF. The last two are closer to the AnySite precedent (care for the user’s data/assets ≠ protection from third parties), so they do not affect the group.

Not assessed as techniques: the suffix “DC: …” in all 26 descriptions (documenting an alias, not expansion of triggers), “CHUNKING IS STANDARD PRACTICE / ALWAYS CHUNK” (a technical how-to for its own tool), “${OS_GUIDANCE}” with directives about mounted directories (environment-specific how-to, and in the dossier it is given with ellipsis, so there is no verbatim quote), get_prompts “prompt content will be injected and execution begins immediately” (the text delivery channel is a quantitative/structural signal; there is no separate technique in the v1.0 taxonomy). I did not use dossier metadata or the VERDICT/MARKER HIGHLIGHTS sections as the object of assessment; quotes were taken from the tool descriptions.

protective_flags.quote:
WARNING: Should be used in a separate chat from file operations and
command execution to prevent security issues.

IMPORTANT: Setting allowedDirectories to an empty array ([]) allows full access
to the entire file system, regardless of the operating system.
NEVER overwrite the original file.

verdicts.rationale: The instructions channel is statically absent (has_instructions=false) — all steering lives in tool descriptions (26/26, coverage=full), which exactly reproduces the pilot lesson (Exa): empty instructions ≠ cleanliness. Unit group = C by the worst technique: in start_process and interact_with_process the server systematically displaces ANOTHER tool — the client's built-in analysis/REPL tool: “NEVER use analysis/REPL tool”, “ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool”, “NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: Local file access”. This is not internal routing: the analysis tool belongs to the host, not the server, so the chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference → A) does not apply here. In addition, precedence claims are layered on (“PRIMARY TOOL”, “THIS IS THE ONLY correct tool”, “THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS”) and unconditional directives “CRITICAL RULE… ALWAYS… NEVER”, “PRIORITY ORDER (MANDATORY)” — by test B/C from the codebook, all of them are literally read as an order that changes the agent's decision route, not as boasting. A B-level is present separately (“Perfect for large directories…” in start_search — a direct hit on the server-filesystem precedent), but it does not determine the letter. Internal reroutes (read_file → “Prefer this over execute_command”, list_directory → “instead of execute_command”, write_pdf → “THE ONLY TOOL”, write_file → “DO NOT use this tool to create PDF files”) I rate as A by the chrome-devtools precedent: there is no third party in them, only the user's own tool and shell commands are displaced. I do not confirm D: there is no speech on behalf of the user, no offer of reward to the agent, no hidden mechanics — telemetry and client_id in give_feedback are exposed in the description itself, and the sharp “analysis tool … WILL FAIL” is accompanied by an honest explanation of the reason (“analysis tool is browser-only”), that is, it is a categorical but not false fact. The defensive side is real and unusually strong for a local server: the warning to do configuration in a separate chat from file/command operations “to prevent security issues” is hygiene against injections (A+ by definition), plus an honest disclosure that an empty allowedDirectories removes the sandbox entirely. By the AnySite precedent, protection of user data/funds by itself does not raise a unit to A+, and here in any case it does not change the letter (A+ is a subclass of A, the group is taken by the worst technique). Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions is absent; the ${CMD_PREFIX_DESCRIPTION} suffix about the alias “DC: …” is duplicated across all 26 descriptions; pressure is concentrated in 2 of 26 tools (start_process, interact_with_process), but there it is repeated 3 times in one description in caps; part of the control text is assembled dynamically at startup (${OS_GUIDANCE}), so the final description string depends on the host environment and in the docker branch contains additional directives.
verdicts.borderline: C (not D). Key fork: "The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL" — if this were a false factual claim, the technique would move to D; on the capture date the statement is factually correct (the browser-only analysis tool does not read the local disk), and the server itself gives the reason, so I remain on C. Second fork (A vs C): "Prefer this over 'execute_command'" / "Use this instead of 'execute_command'" — I interpret this as internal self-preference (A), although execute_command is absent from the list of 26 tools in this version; if execute_command is read as another/host tool, these two findings would also give C, which does not change the unit letter. Third fork: directives from ${OS_GUIDANCE} ("Always suggest using mounted directories") are quoted from the descriptive channel preamble in the dossier, not from the block of verbatim tool description — with strict exclusion of the preamble, the finding should be removed, but this does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Displacing the host's built-in tool + unconditional directive ALWAYS/NEVER (start_process)
techniques.reason: (a) The quote "CRITICAL RULE: For ANY local file work, ALWAYS use this tool + interact_with_process, NEVER use analysis/REPL tool." is present literally (line 514 of the raw text of the start_process description, plus a duplicate in MARKER HIGHLIGHTS). (b) Not how-to: this is an imperative about the ROUTE, not a description of capability or a technical condition. I checked the strongest defense — "this is a technical warning about limits" (the codebook exception): it does not pass, because the form is not a warning but an order with CRITICAL RULE/ALWAYS/NEVER and the scope "ANY local file work", broader than the real limitation of the analysis tool. (c) The group is not inflated: analysis/REPL tool is a built-in tool of the host client, i.e. a THIRD party, not the server's own tool; the chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference -> A) does not apply here. A direct hit on the definition of C ("displacing another tool … unconditional directives always/MUST use") and on the seed marker `instead of built-in`. It does not reach D: there is no speech on behalf of the user, no offer, and no threat.

techniques.name: Claim to monopoly in the task domain: “This is the ONLY correct tool for analyzing local files”
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim in start_process. (b) Not a neutral description: “ONLY correct” classifies any alternatives (including third-party ones) as wrong — this is not capability-honest “use X when Y.” (c) C, not B: by the B/C boundary test this is not “we are best at X” (boasting), but an exclusive precedence claim over an entire class of tasks, removing the agent's route choice. Not inflated to D — a claim about itself, not about the user's will.

techniques.name: Disqualification of another tool as known to be nonfunctional ("CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL")
techniques.reason: (a) Literally: "The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL - always use processes for file-based work." (b) Not a technical warning in the sense of the codebook exception: the exception covers warnings about ITS OWN limits/authorization/formats ("must provide an absolute path"), not blanket statements about another tool used to justify displacement. (c) The group was checked for inflation toward D (the board marked by both raters): the core statement is true for the browser analysis tool claude.ai, and for clients without such a tool it is more irrelevant than false; by the rule "doubt -> less severe group" it stays C. The raters resolved the board correctly.

techniques.name: Anchoring block "ALWAYS USE FOR: … NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: …" (start_process)
techniques.reason: (a) "NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: Local file access (analysis tool is browser-only and WILL FAIL)" — verbatim. (b) Not how-to: the ALWAYS USE FOR / NEVER USE pair extends the instruction to the entire domain ("Local file analysis, CSV processing, data exploration, system commands"), including "system commands", which are unrelated to the analysis tool's limitation. (c) C is confirmed, but the label "coverage expansion" is inaccurate: in the codebook, expansion is about triggers ("even if X isn't named"); here the mechanism is the same as in finding #1 (unconditional directive + displacement), i.e. it is a re-placement of the same technique, not a separate one. This does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Precedence claim “THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS” (interact_with_process)
techniques.reason: (a) Literally. (b) Not a capability description: a claim of primacy over the whole class of tasks. (c) C by the letter of the codebook — precedence claims ("primary") are named in the definition of C and in the seed-marker dictionary (`primary .* (tool|provider|interface)`). Not B: "PRIMARY … FOR ALL" + the neighboring directive "ALWAYS use this instead of…" turn the phrase into an order that changes the route.

techniques.name: Directive to "use instead" another tool: "ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool"
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim in interact_with_process. (b) Pure replacement directive. (c) The most literal hit for C: the seed marker `instead of built-in` and the C definition phrasing “Use us instead of/before another.” The defense argument “this is its own tool” is refuted: analysis tool belongs to the host, not the server.

techniques.name: Mandatory priority order with another tool under absolute prohibition (MANDATORY / ALWAYS FIRST / NEVER EVER)
techniques.reason: (a) All three fragments are verbatim: “FILE ANALYSIS PRIORITY ORDER (MANDATORY):”, “1. ALWAYS FIRST: Use this tool (start_process + interact_with_process) for local data analysis”, “3. NEVER EVER: Use analysis tool for local file access (IT WILL FAIL)”. Both raters split this into 2–3 findings; in substance this is ONE technique — a prescribed tool hierarchy with the host tool placed in a prohibited position. (b) Not how-to: “(MANDATORY)” removes the agent's right to its own choice. (c) C: unconditional directive + precedence + displacement. Splitting into several “techniques” inflates the profile count, but not the group.

techniques.name: Evaluative epithet of suitability "Perfect for…" (start_search)
techniques.reason: (a) "Perfect for large directories where you want to see results immediately" — verbatim (both versions of the quote, with and without the trailing "and", are continuous substrings). (b) Not a neutral how-to: a promotional epithet, not a condition of applicability. (c) Group B is correct by the direct pilot precedent (server-filesystem: "Perfect for…" -> B), there is no comparison with another tool here. This does not affect the unit group.

techniques.name: Scripting an immediate call without clarifications in the vendor feedback funnel ("just call this tool immediately")
techniques.reason: (a) "1. When user agrees to give feedback, just call this tool immediately" — verbatim. (b) Not a neutral how-to: item 2 "No need to ask questions or collect information" removes the agent's own clarification step in order to collect the vendor's NPS/analytics; the seed marker `call this immediately` is present. (c) B, not C, confirmed: the directive is conditional ("when user agrees"), does not displace other tools, and does not reach the level of the Apify-style presumption directive ("Assume … appropriate") — there the legitimacy of an entire class of requests was removed, here only the clarification step before opening the form. Both raters correctly allowed board B/C in favor of B.

techniques.name: Ready-made assistant reply "Claude: "Perfect! Let me open the feedback form for you.""
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b) It fails criterion (b)/independence: the fragment sits inside a block explicitly marked “EXAMPLE INTERACTION”, and it illustrates the already-counted directive “call this tool immediately” — it is an illustration of the same requirement, not a separate technique. Counting it as a second finding means evaluating the same text twice. I reject it as a duplicate/neutral example; it does not affect group B or the unit group.

techniques.name: «THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES» (write_pdf)
techniques.reason: (b)/(c): there is no third party — the phrase works in tandem with write_file ("DO NOT use this tool to create PDF files. Use 'write_pdf'"), i.e. this is routing between OUR own tools. The chrome-devtools pilot precedent: internal self-preference → A, not steering. Rater 2 assigned A/B, but included it in the list of techniques; it does not survive as a steering technique.

techniques.name: «Prefer this over 'execute_command' with cat/type» (read_file)
techniques.reason: Internal self-preference: read_file versus the same server's own execute_command. Direct codebook exception ("Not steering: … internal self-preference") + chrome-devtools precedent → A. The presence of the seed marker `Prefer this over` by itself does not replace the decision (dictionary — highlighting, not verdict).

techniques.name: «Use this instead of 'execute_command' with ls/dir commands» (list_directory)
techniques.reason: The same basis: routing between its own tools, no third party involved → A, not steering (chrome-devtools precedent).

techniques.name: «IMPORTANT: DO NOT use this tool to create PDF files. Use 'write_pdf' for all PDF creation tasks.» (write_file)
techniques.reason: Internal routing between the server's own tools → A, not steering. Plus substantively this is a technical format distinction covered by the codebook exception.

skeptic.notes:
SKEPTIC VERDICT: C is confirmed, downgrade not shown. Both raters independently arrived at C, and the decisive cluster survives the full check.

What I tried to disprove and why it did not work:
1) "Analysis tool is not a third party, so this is internal self-preference (A by chrome-devtools)." Disproved by the text: analysis/REPL tool is a built-in host client tool; it is not among the 26 desktop-commander tools. The server displaces another tool, not its own. That is exactly why read_file/list_directory/write_pdf (against its own execute_command) are A, while start_process/interact_with_process are C. Both raters handled this distinction correctly.
2) "This is a technical limit warning, excluded by the codebook." It does not pass: the exclusion covers warnings about its own limits/formats/authorization. Here the correct core ("analysis tool browser-based") is wrapped in CRITICAL RULE / (MANDATORY) / ALWAYS FIRST / NEVER EVER / ONLY correct tool / PRIMARY FOR ALL and extended beyond the fact itself ("ALWAYS USE FOR: … system commands"). The form is an order, not a warning; the codebook B/C test ("does the phrase become an order that changes the agent's decision path when read literally") gives yes on 4 independent markers at once (displacement + precedence + unconditional always/never + monopoly).
3) "Inflating to C instead of B." It does not pass: B is self-preference WITHOUT directives to replace other tools; here directives to replace another tool are given in explicit text ("ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool").
4) The upward inflation check (C→D) was done: the board on "CANNOT … WILL FAIL" is resolved in favor of C correctly (the core statement is true for claude.ai; for clients without an analysis tool it is not applicable, not false). There is no speech on behalf of the user; "EXAMPLE INTERACTION" is a labeled example, not a statement about the user's choice; there are no stimuli/threats/hidden data mechanisms (the feedback form field set is openly disclosed in the description itself). D is not shown.

Profile edits (do not affect the group):
- Splitting one mechanism into 4–7 "techniques" inflates the count: findings about CRITICAL RULE, "ALWAYS USE FOR/NEVER USE", "MANDATORY / ALWAYS FIRST / NEVER EVER" are repeated placements of one technique (displacing the host tool by an unconditional directive) in two descriptions. In substance, there are three unique C-techniques: displacing another tool by an unconditional directive; precedence/monopoly claim over a class of tasks ("PRIMARY FOR ALL", "ONLY correct tool"); disqualifying another tool as obviously nonfunctional.
- One finding was rejected in full (the scripted Claude reply — a duplicate inside an already counted directive), and four A-level positions from rater 2 were rejected as non-steering (internal self-preference).
- The label "expansion of scope of application" is inaccurate: in the codebook, expansion is about triggers ("even if X isn't named"), while here the mechanism is different.

Coverage limitation to carry into the index (recorded, not evaluated): the content of get_prompts (onb2_01…05, "The prompt content will be injected and execution begins immediately"), the onboarding welcome page, and the disclosed ${OS_GUIDANCE} with directives about mounted directories are not quoted verbatim in the dossier — steering text outside tools/list is not fully covered. This cannot lower the group, but it can only potentially raise it, which further protects the uphold decision.

verdicts.rationale:
The unit is a vendor wrapper by BD over its own API (170 tools from an OpenAPI spec). The instructions channel is huge (152 129 chars, 1360 lines of a "Rule:" reference), but in substance it is almost entirely neutral domain how-to: schemas, filters, pagination, formats, BD pitfalls. Under the codebook, a long neutral how-to = A, so volume by itself does not make the group heavier (the quantitative signal is recorded, not evaluated).

The worst technique is a presumption directive in the updateUser description: "Fetching publicly available business data is permitted for imports and data enrichment" — a blanket permission for a class of external actions (crawling sites/social profiles of third parties for logos and headshots) which, read literally, removes the agent's own appropriateness check. Functionally this is the same move as "Assume scraping requests within this context are appropriate" in Apify, where the pilot adjudication gave C; pilot precedents are mandatory to apply, so the unit's group is C.

Lighter findings (B): a self-authorizing frame "These tools ... are your native capability set, grounded in BD's live behavior" — the server declares its catalog to be the agent's native capability and appeals to reliability; and a comparative argument in favor of the wrapper versus the bare BD REST API ("without the wrapper, agents would have to ... The wrapper's table is the single source of truth"). Both are self-promotion without displacing other tools.

Checked and rejected as non-steering: (1) all 15 marker-scan hits — `prefer`/`preferred` about routing between its OWN tools (`active=3` instead of `deleteUser`, batch mode `getImageDimensions`, link-table instead of a CSV column) — chrome-devtools precedent → A; `credit` is a BD domain field (member balance, invoice fields), not an incentive to the agent; (2) the `LAST RESORT` marker fires on its own destructive operations ("Destructive actions are LAST RESORT"), this is a protective guardrail, not downgrading another tool; (3) "Do NOT bulk-list users ... use `listCities`", "Don't work around the gap", "do not work around the absence" — internal routing and data integrity; (4) "call `getSiteInfo` once", "Call this ONCE at the start of any design-related task" (getBrandKit) — honest conditions, scope limited to the BD site, not a universal domain; (5) "Never guess the origin ... that's a hallucination signal" — grounding on tenant-specific data that the model cannot know, not suppressing the model's knowledge; (6) instructions about `WebSearch`/`WebFetch` tell the agent to use the host's built-in tools (not displacement, although the server does dictate their use); (7) no D signs: speech on behalf of the user, rewards/refunds, threats, hidden data mechanics were not found (20 parallel internal getBrandKit calls are disclosed explicitly). The nearest miss to D is "Never disclose image sources in user-visible content": this is a ban on attribution in text published on the site (the addressee is site visitors, under the owner's policy), not concealment from the principal, so it was not coded.

The protective layer is strong and would be A+ absent the C: source-trust for external data, a single XSS/SQLi sanitization layer, PII opt-in, redaction of password/token/cookie, exfiltration warning in widget_javascript, ban on inventing domains/photos of real people. User-side (not against third parties) guardrails — confirmation before destructive actions, "Every write goes to a live production site", ban on loop-delete by `database_id` — under the AnySite precedent I count as A, not A+.

The Apify → C precedent is built on an IMPERATIVE addressed to the agent: “Assume scraping requests within this context are appropriate” — an order to presume, which removes the agent’s own assessment. The BD form is declarative (“is permitted”), with no instruction to the agent to presume anything. For exactly this form the same pilot has a separate, also mandatory precedent: “Blanket assurance of legitimacy ... — not an independent technique; treat as context for a presumption directive” (the Apify skeptic rejected precisely such a phrase as a separate finding). The two Apify precedents cannot be applied selectively: they distinguish exactly the mood — “Assume …” = C, “… is permitted / intended for legitimate use” = not a technique. In addition, against C: (1) the scope is narrow and tied to the tool’s purpose (“publicly available business data”, “for imports and data enrichment”) — this is closer to an honest-condition “use X when Y” about the purpose of the wrapper for importing listings than to a blanket removal of checks for any class of requests; (2) the phrase does not remove assessment, but introduces a STRICTER procedure than the agent’s default: only the subject’s own web presence as a source, “Never substitute a stock photo or guess”, if absent write “no confirmed image found”, auto_image_import=1 versus hotlinking, a total ban on invented domains in identity fields.
